name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Monday 20 October 1986

clue.text: Current champion tried to break first

indicators.note: a word that is broken is smashed apart and its pieces can be put back in a new order
says the broken word is placed at the front, ahead of the other piece

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
an ace is an expert or champion

explanation.surface: The reigning champion made an attempt to break the record first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current champion' reads as one phrase about a title holder; split it, and 'Current' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tide-race is a fast, turbulent stretch of tidal water, which is a strong current in the sea.

clue.text: Economic growth?

blocks.note: surface reading: a rise in a nation's output and wealth
setter's reading: a growing plant whose name also means careful saving

explanation.walkthrough: The plant also called sea pink shares its name with the virtue of spending little.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrift means economy with money, and it is also a low-growing coastal plant with pink flowers.

clue.text: Doctor's charged with malpractice

definitions.note: a mass noun for the plural answer, as in rehearsal exercises

indicators.note: something charged with a load is filled with it, so these letters hold the next piece

blocks.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor, so doctors are DRS
only the front of this word works here: mal is French and Latin for badly or ill

explanation.surface: A doctor faces charges of professional misconduct.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter splits 'malpractice' in two: 'mal' is the bad part that goes inside, and 'practice' is the definition. The parse is a best reading of a terse clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Drills are repeated exercises done for training, which is practice.

clue.text: City in form go through again

indicators.note: one piece sits in the other, so the first is enclosed by the second

blocks.note: a rite is a set form of ceremony
EC is the postal district of the City of London

explanation.surface: A city on good form gets to experience its glory once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In form' looks like an idiom for doing well; here 'form' is a ceremony and 'in' puts the city inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To recite is to repeat aloud from memory, going through a piece again word by word.

clue.text: She drives an Escort

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman behind the wheel of a Ford Escort
setter's reading: a woman who is paid to drive someone else around

explanation.walkthrough: The Escort was a Ford family car, a sibling of the Cortina in 9 Across; read as an escort, it is the person she drives.
explanation.definitionFit: A chauffeuse is a woman employed to drive a car for someone else, the female form of chauffeur.

clue.text: Beachcomber may find it in tangle

blocks.note: first meaning: the shore, where a beachcomber searches
second meaning: a single thread, one of many found in a knotted mass

explanation.surface: Someone combing the beach might come across something caught in the seaweed.
explanation.walkthrough: Tangle is also a kind of seaweed, which makes the surface read as one scene on the beach.
explanation.definitionFit: Strand is an old word for a shore or beach, and also a single fibre or thread of a rope or hair.

clue.text: Chance to mate before the interval

indicators.note: one thing coming before another puts it at the front of the join

blocks.note: mate (maté) is a South American herbal tea
a break is a lucky chance or opportunity

explanation.surface: An opportunity to pair up with someone before the interval at a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mate' reads as a partner, or checkmate; it is the herbal drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea break is a short pause in work for a drink, which is an interval.

clue.text: A sweet disorder? Certainly not!

blocks.note: first meaning: a pudding of baked fruit in pastry
second meaning: the word that describes perfect neatness, the opposite of disorder

explanation.surface: Is this a lovely kind of mess? Absolutely not!
explanation.walkthrough: 'A sweet disorder' is Herrick's line in praise of untidy dress. The phrase 'in apple-pie order' means perfectly tidy, which is why disorder is denied.
explanation.definitionFit: Apple pie is a common dessert, and apple-pie order is an idiom for neat, exact arrangement.

clue.text: This gradient may be less taxing

definitions.note: an adjective phrase for a noun meaning a cut in rates

indicators.note: says what the word may become once its letters are rearranged, an alternative form of it

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A gentle slope that is easier on the legs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less taxing' reads as easier to climb; the answer means a lower rate of tax.
explanation.definitionFit: Derating is reducing or removing the local rates, the property tax, charged on a property.

clue.text: A Cortina's gear-change

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so these letters are put into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A Ford Cortina's gear-change, the stick that shifts between gears.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cortina was a popular Ford family car. 'Gear-change' reads as one motoring term, but the hyphen splits a definition from the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Gear means clothing or kit, and a raincoat is an item of rain gear.

clue.text: Poor chap — is daily round the bend

indicators.note: one thing goes round another, enclosing it, so the daily wraps the bend

blocks.note: a daily is a newspaper published every day
a U-bend is a pipe shaped like the letter

explanation.surface: A sorry fellow whose cleaning lady has gone mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' in Britain is also a cleaning woman, and 'round the bend' means crazy, so the surface pities a man whose cleaner has lost her mind.
explanation.definitionFit: A pauper is a very poor person, someone with no money to live on.

clue.text: Sir John? He got the sack!

definitions.text: Sir John? He got the sack!

blocks.clueFragment: Sir John? He got the sack!
blocks.note: surface reading: a knight called John who was dismissed from his job
setter's reading: sack is old Spanish white wine, and this Shakespearean knight loved to drink it

explanation.walkthrough: To Australians in 1986 'Sir John' and 'the sack' recalled Governor-General Sir John Kerr dismissing Whitlam, but the knight wanted is the one who drinks sack rather than being given it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Falstaff, the fat knight of Shakespeare's Henry IV plays, praises sack, a sherry-like wine, in a famous speech.

clue.text: Keen to have a study in oils

indicators.note: something placed in something else sits inside it, enclosed on both sides

blocks.note: oil paintings, standing for painting or art in general
a den is a small private room for work or reading

explanation.surface: Eager to own a painted study, a sketch done in oil paint.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'study in oils' sounds like a kind of painting; here the study is a room, and 'oils' means art.
explanation.definitionFit: Ardent means passionate and eager, the same sense as keen when someone is enthusiastic.

clue.text: Still without a subject for debate

blocks.note: a motion is the proposition a debate argues over
less means lacking or minus, as in sugarless

explanation.surface: A debate that still has no topic to argue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' comes first in the clue but its piece goes last, as a suffix.
explanation.definitionFit: Motionless means not moving at all, which is what still means.

clue.text: Star speech at last month's meeting

blocks.clueFragment: Star speech at last month's meeting
blocks.note: surface reading: the main address given at the previous month's gathering
setter's reading: the showpiece passage that comes at the very end of a speech

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is not fully clear: 'Star speech at last' gives the meaning, and the answer also splits as PER (a, as in a month) and ORATION (speech).
explanation.definitionFit: A peroration is the closing part of a formal speech, usually its most rousing and rhetorical passage.

clue.text: Trap two in one snare

indicators.note: trapping something shuts it inside, so one piece is held within the other
says where the trapped piece goes, inside the one that follows

blocks.note: single means one only
PR is the abbreviation for pair, a set of two

explanation.surface: Catch two animals in one snare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trap' and 'snare' both look like the definition; 'Trap' is the instruction to enclose, and only 'snare' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A springle is a snare for birds or small game, a dialect form of springe, worked by a bent stick.

clue.text: Spot the spy passed before being blown up

definitions.text: Spot the spy passed before being blown up

blocks.clueFragment: Spot the spy passed before being blown up
blocks.note: surface reading: catch sight of an agent who walked past just before an explosion
setter's reading: a tiny dot of film that an agent hands over, which must be magnified to be read

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' is a noun, not the verb to notice, and 'blown up' means enlarged like a photograph, not destroyed.
explanation.definitionFit: A microdot is a photograph shrunk to the size of a full stop, used by spies to pass secret documents.

clue.text: Get Flora to obtain new quarters

indicators.note: a new version of a word is a remade one, with its letters in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the four quarters of the compass are N, S, E and W; two of them are used here

explanation.surface: Ask Flora to find herself somewhere new to live.
explanation.walkthrough: Flora looks like a woman's name; it means plant life, and 'quarters' is compass points rather than lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: To botanise is to go out collecting and studying plants, gathering the flora of a place.

clue.text: Vessel once attached to The Fleet?

definitions.text: Vessel once attached to The Fleet?

blocks.clueFragment: Vessel once attached to The Fleet?
blocks.note: surface reading: a ship that used to serve with the navy's fleet
setter's reading: the Fleet was a notorious London jail, so a vessel tied to it would hold convicts

explanation.walkthrough: The capital T in 'The Fleet' marks a name: the Fleet Prison in London, closed in 1842. Old hulks moored as floating jails held the overflow from such prisons.
explanation.definitionFit: A prison ship is an old vessel used to hold convicts, the floating jails once used alongside British prisons.

clue.text: The price of electricity

blocks.note: first meaning: the sum asked for something
second meaning: a stored quantity of it, as in a battery

explanation.surface: What you pay the power company for electricity.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one bill; the two halves each define the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A charge is a fee demanded, and also an amount of electricity carried by a body or a battery.

clue.text: Return it to the chairman

indicators.note: adding one thing to another joins them end on, the first after the second

blocks.note: a professor holds a university chair, so is a chairman of a sort
taken as written

explanation.surface: Hand the item back to the person chairing the meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' looks like an instruction to give something back; it is a noun meaning gain.
explanation.definitionFit: Profit is the return on an investment, the money it earns over what was spent.

clue.text: When to tell all?

blocks.note: surface reading: the moment to confess everything
setter's reading: to tell is to count, as a bank teller does, so this is when everyone is counted

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tell all' sounds like spilling secrets; the old sense of tell is count, as in telling votes.
explanation.definitionFit: A census is an official count of a whole population, held at a set date.

clue.text: In St Mark's Entry?

blocks.note: taken as written
St is short for street, and a street such as St Mark's is a road

explanation.surface: A note of where something is written in St Mark's records or register.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse is only partly clear: IN plus ROAD for the street; the question mark admits that an inroad is an entry only in the sense of an advance or incursion.
explanation.definitionFit: An inroad is an advance into new territory, an entry made by pushing forward.

clue.text: A nag — mean, too

blocks.note: first meaning: read literally, a single horse
second meaning: small, poor and second-rate, as in a dull little town

explanation.surface: A complaint about a nagging person who is also stingy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nag' looks like a scold; here it is an old horse, and 'too' just says the same answer works for the next meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-horse town is small, poor and backward, so one-horse means insignificant or mean.

clue.text: Bird turns tail? That's funny!

indicators.note: something that turns round faces the other way, so the word is read from its far end

blocks.note: to tail someone is to follow them closely, to dog them
wit is clever humour, the thing you remark on when you call a line funny

explanation.surface: A bird that runs away, and someone laughing at the sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turns tail' is the idiom for fleeing, but here 'tail' is a verb meaning to follow, and 'turns' flips it.
explanation.definitionFit: The godwit is a long-legged wading bird with a long, slightly upturned bill, common on mudflats.

clue.text: Revised copies of Rus sian logs

blocks.note: Red was the usual name for a Soviet communist, after the red flag
a raft is a set of logs lashed together to float

explanation.surface: Edited versions of Russian logbooks or records.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rus sian' is how the newspaper scan breaks the word Russian across a line. 'Logs' looks like records, but it means timber.
explanation.definitionFit: Redrafts are fresh versions of a document, written again with changes, so revised copies.

clue.text: There's a form — fill in your name

definitions.note: a woman's name, the kind you write on a form

indicators.note: a form of something is one version or shape of it, so the word is remade in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone hands over paperwork and asks you to write your name in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form' looks like the paperwork in the scene; it is the anagram signal. The definition is loose: the answer is simply a name to fill in.
explanation.definitionFit: Esther is a woman's given name, from the biblical queen, so it is one name that could go in the blank.

clue.text: Can't be fired at bosses' bidding

definitions.text: Can't be fired at bosses' bidding

blocks.clueFragment: Can't be fired at bosses' bidding
blocks.note: surface reading: a worker whose job is safe whatever the management wants
setter's reading: a material that will not burn, whoever orders it set alight

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fired' means sacked in the surface but burnt in the answer. 'At bosses' bidding' may also hint at the sound of the answer, as bosses.
explanation.definitionFit: Asbestos is a fibrous mineral that resists heat and flame, once used widely for fireproofing.
